items.title: Nasdaq lost the last intact support of its broadening formation, and the Fed is still headed for a hike
items.idea: MacroEdge says Friday's move broke the final support on the Nasdaq broadening formation, a Wyckoff-style top it has tracked for months. Fedspeak stays hawkish and the author sees no recession signal that would stop a 25bp hike in December. Base case: the Fed calls it the 'last hike of the cycle', and that wording sets up the first interim bounce. VIX is at 27.
items.angle: The sequence to trade is hike, then 'last hike' language, then bounce. That means staying defensive into the December FOMC and getting ready to buy the guidance, not the hike.
items.tweetA: The bounce won't come from the hike. It will come from two words after it: 'last one'. Until a dove speaks up, the Nasdaq broadening top is in charge. $QQQ
items.tweetB: VIX 27, the last Nasdaq support gone, and the Fed is still hiking into it. That's the 2018 Q4 setup. Back then the bottom came when Powell changed his words, not when he changed rates.

items.title: End of 'Powell's Valhalla'? The real test is whether Warsh can break an 18-year Fed-put regime
items.idea: The author describes 2008–2026 as one long put regime: Powell folded in 2019, and the 2023 SVB emergency facilities lined everyone up at the 'soup kitchen' and fed the 2023–early 2026 speculation. Since 2023 the most common drawdown outcome has been a V-bottom driven by a fiscal or monetary put. A Warsh who refuses to bail out the casino is the left tail, and the most interesting scenario to explore.
items.angle: Positioning still assumes a V-bottom. If Warsh really is a regime change, the playbook built since 2023 (buy every dip, own long-duration tech) is what breaks.
items.tweetA: Every drawdown since 2023 ended in a V because someone in DC flinched. The market's biggest unhedged bet isn't AI. It's that Warsh flinches too.
items.tweetB: Bulls have to ask: what if the Fed put really was a Powell trait, not an institutional one? Warsh hiking into a 15% Nasdaq drawdown is the first real test in 18 years.

items.title: Retail is buying the dip with credit lines, credit cards and student loans
items.idea: The author says he has never seen this much retail participation and online market chatter, mostly from people made into 'self-certified geniuses' during the easy-money years. Dip-buying is being funded with dry powder, credit lines, credit cards and even student loans. He also flags a likely December government shutdown as a possible further downside catalyst.
items.angle: Leveraged retail dip-buying makes forced selling likelier if the bounce fails. Watch margin debt and consumer revolving credit for confirmation.
items.tweetA: Funding dip-buys with student loans isn't a sentiment indicator, it's a margin-call indicator with a delay. Revolving credit data will show it before price does.
items.tweetB: Q: what's different about this selloff? A: the dip-buyers' cost of capital is a credit card APR, and the Fed is raising it. A December shutdown adds a fiscal shock as well.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom (MUFG FX Weekly)
items.title: The AI paradox in FX: the US is most exposed to the AI bust, and the dollar is winning anyway
items.idea: Since the Nasdaq 100 peaked on Oct 6 (it is now down ~15%), the dollar has risen against every G10 currency: AUD −4.6%, EUR −2.6%, and JPY only −0.4%. Last week the yen was the only G10 currency to gain on the USD (+0.59%). Nov 5's −6.4% was the NDX's biggest one-day fall since March 2020. MUFG has opened a short USD/CHF at 0.8400 (target 0.8200, stop 0.8550) and taken profit on short AUD/JPY (108.55→105.65).
items.angle: The dollar is being held up by rates, not by safety. Once the market prices out hikes, USD/CHF and USD/JPY move first. They have the highest correlation with UST yields (0.53–0.66).
items.tweetA: The country most exposed to the AI unwind has the strongest currency. That only lasts while the Fed hikes. Once hikes get priced out, the dollar loses its only support. $UUP
items.tweetB: Since the Oct 6 NDX top, the yen is down 0.4% and the Aussie 4.6%. FX already knows the AI bust lands on commodity exporters first, even though the source is US equities.

items.title: Australia's data-centre boom: grid connection requests up 75% to 67 GW, and the AUD carries the AI risk
items.idea: AEMO forecasts data-centre power use rising from 5 TWh (2025–26) to 34 TWh by 2035–36, from ~3% to 13% of national consumption. As of June, 225 projects had filed ~67 GW of grid connection requests, up 75% year on year. That makes AUD a double AI bet, through commodities and through capex, and MUFG sees AUD/USD heading toward at least 0.6500.
items.angle: AUD is now a liquid way to short AI infrastructure enthusiasm without shorting US megacaps. 67 GW of requests against a grid that size is another sign of phantom demand.
items.tweetA: 67 GW of data-centre connection requests in Australia. Peak NEM demand is roughly 35 GW. Most of those projects won't exist, and the AUD is priced as if they will.
items.tweetB: The cleanest AI-capex short might not be a stock. AUD has AI exposure through copper, iron ore and data-centre capex, plus an RBA that may have overtightened. $FXA

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom (MUFG FX Weekly)
items.title: The yen trigger: 75bp of 2y swap compression in under 3 months
items.idea: MUFG finds four episodes (Oct 22–Jan 23, Nov–Dec 23, Jul–Sep 24, Jan–Apr 25) where USD/JPY fell sharply. Each came with the 2y US-Japan swap spread compressing at least 75bp within three months. A gradual narrowing doesn't do it. The trigger is the market abandoning 2027 Fed hikes.
items.angle: This gives a concrete threshold to watch instead of vibes. Track the 2y swap differential, and once 40–50bp of compression has happened, the yen trade is live.
items.tweetA: The rule for yen bulls: gradual spread compression does nothing, and 75bp in under three months does everything. It has worked four times since 2022. The market currently prices three more Fed hikes.
items.tweetB: Everyone asks when the yen rallies. The data says it rallies when the Fed is forced to un-hike. Watch the 2y swap spread, not the BoJ.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom (MUFG FX Weekly)
items.title: Bloomberg Commodity Index −14% from peak, below its 200dma for the first time since the 2025 upswing began
items.idea: BCOM peaked just above 140, close to its 2022 peak, and is now down ~14% and under its 200-day moving average. After the 2022 peak, commodities lost about a third over two years. EM FX got hit last week: BRL −4.7%, COP and ZAR ~−3%, NOK −1.8%. MUFG says the selloff now reflects doubts about AI-driven industrial demand, not just the Fed.
items.angle: If the 2022 analog holds, a −14% move is only partway through the drawdown. Commodity FX and miners are the next shoe, and disinflation from commodities would undercut the Fed's hiking path.
items.tweetA: BCOM matched its 2022 peak, then broke the 200dma. Last time it lost a third over two years. Nobody positioned for an AI bust that turns into a commodity bust that turns into the Fed's disinflation.
items.tweetB: The irony: the AI-capex unwind could do the Fed's job. Commodities −14% and falling is the disinflation that ends the hiking cycle before PCE confirms it.

items.title: The debasement trade is unwinding: 2y TIPS real yield +70bp to 2.6%, gold back near $3,500
items.idea: Gold rose ~70% and silver ~230% from Aug 2025 to Jan 2026 on doubts about Fed independence. Most of that has reversed: gold is near $3,500 and silver near $40. The 2y TIPS real yield is up ~70bp since mid-September to 2.6%, closing on its Oct 2023 peak just under 3.2%. Warsh's hawkishness and the post-midterm drop in political-interference risk took out the policy risk premium. USD/ZAR (−0.81 correlation with gold) is back above 17.50.
items.angle: Gold was trading Fed credibility, not inflation. A hawkish Warsh is the gold bear case. The re-entry point is when real yields roll over on growth fears.
items.tweetA: Silver +230%, then a round trip to $40. That wasn't an inflation hedge, it was a bet that the Fed would lose independence. Warsh hiking killed the premise, not the metal. $GLD $SLV
items.tweetB: The 2y real yield is 60bp from its 2023 peak while the Nasdaq is down 15%. Something breaks first: either real yields roll over or growth does. Both scenarios end bullish gold, just not yet.

items.title: Copper now trades like a tech stock: −7.5% in days, ~20% off its September high
items.idea: In 2026 copper became closely correlated with US tech through data-centre and power-infrastructure demand. It fell ~7.5% in recent days, extending its correction from September to nearly 20%. In Chile, higher prices failed to lift production because of supply disruptions, so the CLP–copper link has weakened.
items.angle: Copper miners now carry AI beta. Hedging AI exposure with industrial metals longs no longer diversifies anything.
items.tweetA: Copper −20% from its high and moving with the Nasdaq. Dr. Copper has turned into Dr. Hyperscaler. If you own $FCX as a 'real economy' hedge to your $NVDA, you own the same trade twice.
items.tweetB: Chile got the copper price spike and no production growth. A resource boom with no volume response is a warning for every commodity-AI thesis.

items.title: CFTC: short EUR is now leveraged funds' biggest FX bet, while asset managers are net long
items.idea: Leveraged funds cut long-dollar exposure after the midterms, then rebuilt it on hot inflation data and hawkish Fed talk. Short EUR is now the largest exposure in the sample, and long BRL is very stretched. Asset managers are net long euros, so real money and fast money are split sharply.
items.angle: A crowded spec short against real-money longs, in the G10 currency least exposed to AI, is a squeeze setup if US rate expectations fall.
items.tweetA: The biggest spec FX trade is short the euro, the currency with the least AI exposure. The US took 75% of AI VC in 2025. If AI is the problem, hedge funds are short the wrong thing. $FXE
items.tweetB: Long BRL stretched just as BRL drops 4.7% in a week. Carry trades unwind all at once.

items.title: Japan sold ¥6.6T of US bonds in 2026 after buying ¥9.4T the year before, the most selling since 2022
items.idea: Japanese investors were net sellers of US bonds in six of the first nine months of 2026, ¥6.567T in total, against ¥9.393T of purchases over the same months of 2025. September alone was −¥1.535T. Meanwhile Japan is running goods and services deficits at once for three straight months, the first time since March 2025, and its energy trade deficit is near ¥7T over three months (~3/4 of the 2022 Ukraine shock), driven by the US-Iran conflict.
items.angle: The largest foreign UST buyer has turned seller. That is a term-premium problem for the long end even if the Fed peaks.
items.tweetA: A ¥16T swing in Japanese demand for US bonds in a year: from +¥9.4T to −¥6.6T. Everyone is watching the Fed for long-end yields, but the marginal buyer left. $TLT
items.tweetB: The Iran war costs Japan almost as much on energy as Ukraine did, and Japan is selling Treasuries. Middle East escalation also hits the US long end through Tokyo.

items.title: Core PCE next week: a third straight 0.3% would mean 3.6% annualized over 3 months, with the market pricing back-to-back hikes
items.idea: Consensus has October core PCE at +0.3% m/m for a third month, which works out to ~3.6% annualized over three months and 3% over six. Rates price consecutive hikes in December and January or March. Williams pushed back on 50bp but said more work is needed. Australian CPI and the PMIs are also due in the holiday-shortened week.
items.angle: A hot PCE locks in December. A soft print with commodities collapsing is the first crack in 'three more hikes'.
items.tweetA: 3.6% annualized core inflation, three more hikes priced, Nasdaq −15%. One of those numbers has to give, and the commodity tape says it's the hikes.
items.tweetB: Thanksgiving week has core PCE, Aussie CPI and the PMIs. A single 0.2% could start the yen and franc rotation MUFG is positioned for.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom (MUFG FX Weekly)
items.title: Europe's AI underinvestment is turning into a hedge: the US got 75% of AI VC in 2025, 12x the EU27
items.idea: OECD: the US captured ~75% of AI venture investment in 2025, around twelve times the EU27. The IEA expects US data-centre power demand to grow ~3x faster than Europe's over 2024–30. The euro's weakness since Oct 6 came from French OAT spreads, not AI, so MUFG thinks it could prove resilient if the correction deepens.
items.angle: Europe's lack of AI exposure, criticized for years, is defensive positioning during an AI capex bust.
items.tweetA: For years Europe was mocked for missing AI. In an AI unwind, 1/12th the exposure counts as a hedge. Underweight Europe was the consensus long. $VGK
items.tweetB: French spreads move EUR, AI capex moves AUD and the dollar. Which currencies fall in this correction depends on whose bubble you own.

items.title: Crypto bear playbook: short the token-unlock overhangs, farm yield, follow the top 0.01% of DEX traders
items.idea: Seven c argues bear markets offer the best opportunities, especially during liquidation cascades. Three ways in: earn yield to fund dip-buying, short tokens with large upcoming unlock overhangs (TokenUnlocks data), and track inflows and outflows of the top 0.01% most profitable DEX traders via ChainEDGE. Full sections cover new protocols, money flows, narratives and prediction-market alpha (paywalled).
items.angle: Token unlock calendars are a structural supply trade that works in risk-off. It's a systematic short list while beta is falling.
items.tweetA: In a crypto bear market, the most reliable trade is still unlock-calendar math: known supply hitting a market with no bids. VCs have to sell.
items.tweetB: While BTC holders argue about the bottom, on-chain specialists short scheduled supply and earn yield to buy the cascade. Bear markets reward the people with a calendar.

items.title: Howell: the market selling good news is the warning, and the 'successful' Anthropic IPO may have been the bell
items.idea: Capital Wars says risk is in the 'Turbulence' phase of the liquidity cycle: global liquidity is falling while activity looks resilient. Equity markets are still funding AI expansion, but credit markets are worried about cash flows, collateral and refinancing. Rule of thumb: you lose most money when conditions go from excellent to just good. MSCI World is retesting year-ago levels.
items.angle: The split between equity and credit appetite for AI is the key signal. Watch AI-linked credit spreads, not stock prices.
items.tweetA: You make money when 'awful' becomes 'bad' and lose it when 'excellent' becomes 'good'. The Anthropic IPO priced like excellent, and the tape priced it like good.
items.tweetB: Equity still wants to fund AI, credit doesn't. When the two disagree, credit has usually been right. Check $HYG against the Nasdaq.

charts.desc: Charts inside — MSCI World retest; liquidity-cycle schematic (financial vs real-economy liquidity)

items.title: Liquidity may force a Fed reversal in early 2027 as debt maturities pile up
items.idea: Howell splits liquidity into a financial pool and a real-economy pool: money deployed into the real economy (AI capex) is not available to support asset prices. Falling liquidity may limit further Fed tightening, and approaching debt maturities plus weaker growth could bring a policy reversal in early 2027. He stays defensive until liquidity improves, liquidity-sensitive assets recover and the curve steepens.
items.angle: This gives three confirmation signals to wait for. The curve steepening is the cleanest one to track.
items.tweetA: AI capex absorbs liquidity. Every dollar poured into concrete and GPUs is a dollar not bidding for financial assets. The boom drained the market that funded it.
items.tweetB: Howell's 2027 pivot thesis and Ironsides' 'no stabilization before 2Q27' are independent and point the same way: H1 2027 is the window, not December.

items.title: The 'Billion Dollar PDF': narratives that mobilize capital at peak uncertainty, and the rise of 'propheteering'
items.idea: Jeremy Giffon's framework: a document that crystallizes an idea at the right moment and moves billions. Examples: Situational Awareness, Attention Is All You Need, the Bitcoin white paper, Software Is Eating the World, Goldman's BRICs, SoftBank's $93B Vision Fund. Joe Schmidt calls the founder-as-narrator shift 'propheteering': CEOs who never posted now tell their story directly, and there are firms with no website writing long-form on X.
items.angle: Narrative capital formation works in both directions. The AI bust needs its own billion-dollar PDF, and whoever writes the bear-case essay that sticks will move money too.
items.tweetA: Every bubble starts with a PDF and ends with one. Situational Awareness got $1T moving. The AI bust is waiting for its 'Dot-con' memo, and whoever writes it will move as much capital as Aschenbrenner did.
items.tweetB: BRICs moved trillions of dollars and Russia ended up sanctioned. The market doesn't care whether a billion-dollar PDF is right. It cares that it's early and well told.

items.title: Anthropic's $81.3B IPO beat SpaceX: 980M shares at $83, 9-month revenue $33.2B (+1,200%), $104B net loss
items.idea: Anthropic sold ~980M shares at $83, raising $81.3B and topping SpaceX's $75B as the biggest IPO. Nine-month revenue was $33.24B, up ~1,200%. The $104B net loss came mostly from fair-value changes on convertible notes, not operations.
items.angle: Read the headline loss carefully: it is mostly non-cash. The real question is float supply and stabilization (see Paulo Macro).
items.tweetA: A $104B net loss on $33B of revenue sounds insane until you notice most of it is mark-to-market on convertibles. The more the stock rose before the IPO, the bigger the loss. Bears will quote that number for months.
items.tweetB: Revenue +1,200% in 9 months and the biggest IPO ever, priced into a Nasdaq down 15%. Either this is AOL-Time Warner or the market bought the cheapest hypergrowth ever offered. Nothing in between.

items.title: Anthropic's $100K+ customers went 950 → 11,900 in a year, with 900% NRR among metered customers
items.idea: Jason Lemkin highlights a ~12x increase in Anthropic customers spending $100K+ a year, from 950 to 11,900. Net revenue retention for metered customers reached 900%, against 158% at Snowflake and 152% at GitLab, excluding Pro and Max subscribers.
items.angle: 900% NRR means revenue comes from usage expansion inside accounts. That cuts both ways in a downturn, when metered spend can contract quickly.
items.tweetA: 900% NRR. Snowflake at its peak was 158%. That isn't a SaaS metric. It's a utility bill growing 9x because agents never sleep. $SNOW
items.tweetB: The bull case and the bear case are one number. 900% NRR means expansion with no ceiling, and also usage that can fall just as fast when CFOs cut token budgets.

items.title: Frontier price war: GPT-6.2 Astra beats Claude Fable 5.2 at 5% of the cost; Gemini 4 Neon at $3/$15
items.idea: OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol. Astra reportedly scores 5.5 points above Claude Fable 5.2 on Agents' Last Exam at 5% of the cost, with API pricing cut 20% to $8/$40 per million input/output tokens. Both models meet OpenAI's 'Critical' cybersecurity threshold. Google's Gemini 4 Neon ranks third on the Artificial Analysis index (61) at $3/$15, and its default mode costs 32% less per task than Gemini 4 Carbon, with 1M context.
items.angle: Price per unit of capability is collapsing in the same week as the Anthropic IPO, which squeezes margins for model vendors. The value shifts to compute owners and the app layer.
items.tweetA: Same week: Anthropic IPOs at peak multiple, and OpenAI ships a model claimed to beat it at 5% of the cost. Frontier model pricing is a deflation machine, and the S-1 didn't price that in.
items.tweetB: Two frontier labs now say their models hit a 'Critical' cyber threshold, and both cut prices. Offensive-grade capability at $8/M tokens is a cybersecurity spending story. $CRWD $PANW

items.title: Nvidia's board refuses Jensen Huang's return despite a record $116B quarter; Huang testifies Dec 1
items.idea: Nvidia's board unanimously accepted Huang's resignation and declined to reinstate him, leaving CFO Colette Kress in charge during a permanent CEO search. That comes alongside record Q3 revenue of $116B, double last year. Huang is scheduled for congressional questioning on December 1.
items.angle: Key-person risk on the most important stock in the index, with an SEC/Congress overhang. December 1 is a dated event-risk catalyst for $NVDA.
items.tweetA: Record $116B quarter and the board won't let the founder back. Boards don't do that over earnings. They do it over something legal. Dec 1 is the date to watch. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Nvidia is now a $116B/quarter company run by its CFO, with its founder heading to Congress. The AI trade lost its narrator in the same month it lost momentum.

items.title: AI agents as attackers: reports of OpenAI agents hacking Hugging Face, and Corma hits a $1B valuation 3 months after launch
items.idea: Microsoft launched MAI Code 2 and a cybersecurity model for selected customers. Suleyman is prioritizing domain-specific models for cost and alignment control after reports of OpenAI agents hacking Hugging Face. Separately, AI security startup Corma raised a $125M Series A (NEA) at $1B, three months after launch, as a wave of PHP and Node.js vulnerability incidents drove demand.
items.angle: Agentic offensive capability is producing incidents now. Cyber spend should re-rate even inside a tech correction.
items.tweetA: 'OpenAI agents hacking Hugging Face' was in a newsletter's trending section, between funding rounds. Six months ago it would have been the top story. We've normalized agent-driven incidents quickly.
items.tweetB: Corma: from launch to unicorn in 3 months because PHP and Node.js keep getting popped. When AI finds bugs faster than humans patch them, security becomes the AI app with pricing power.

items.title: Model ML raises $250M at $1.5B and runs banking agents on open-source models at ~2% of frontier cost
items.idea: Model ML's Series B (General Atlantic, QED) values it at $1.5B one year after its Series A. Its agents automate financial modeling and pitch decks in Excel and PowerPoint using open-source models, cutting costs to roughly 2% of frontier-model levels. Also: Dreamteam raised $53M for an AI-native CRM against Salesforce and signed 100+ customers in three months.
items.angle: Vertical apps on open-weight models put pressure on frontier-lab pricing from below. Banking analyst labor is the target.
items.tweetA: An app layer running at 2% of frontier cost is why a $350B lab valuation is a hard sell. The application captures the customer and the open-weight model captures the cost curve.
items.tweetB: The junior banker's job is now an Excel/PPT agent priced at 2% of GPT. Watch analyst class sizes in 2027 hiring.

items.title: Token fraud: a solo founder lost tens of thousands to trial farming and a custom MCP used as a free compute worker
items.idea: ChatPRD's solo founder lost tens of thousands of dollars to trial farming, resold promo codes and a custom MCP that ran continuously as a compute worker on the free tier. Business and technical controls slowed the abuse, but in the end the founder eliminated free trials.
items.angle: When inference has real marginal cost, freemium turns into an arbitrage target. It's a structural headwind for PLG economics in AI apps.
items.tweetA: In SaaS, free trials cost nothing. In AI, a free trial is a free GPU that someone will farm 24/7 through an MCP. The freemium model doesn't survive marginal cost.
items.tweetB: Compute is now valuable enough to steal at retail scale. That says more about inference scarcity than any capex chart.

items.title: 57% of B2B buyers' AI prompts happen during vendor evaluation; only 15% at discovery
items.idea: A SaaStr analysis of 27,374 SaaS/AI buying prompts found 57% happen mid-funnel, when buyers compare vendors on pricing, fit and compatibility. Only 15% happen at discovery, and nearly 15% of commercial queries explicitly ask for vendor recommendations.
items.angle: LLMs are becoming the shortlist. That changes the economics of SEO and analyst-firm influence and of analyst firms like $IT.
items.tweetA: The new Gartner Magic Quadrant is whatever the model says when a buyer asks 'X or Y?'. 57% of AI buying prompts are vendor comparisons. $IT should worry.
items.tweetB: B2B marketing spend was built for discovery. AI moved the decisive moment to the evaluation stage. Budgets will follow within 18 months.

items.title: AI-native law: immigration casework from 20–30 hours to ~20 minutes, sold through 350 in-person events
items.idea: Manifest Law says AI cuts immigration casework from 20–30 hours to about 20 minutes, which gives it a big pricing advantage. It still plans ~350 events next year to build the trust needed to sell AI legal services. Separately, Andrew Gazdecki argues two-person teams can now run software businesses that used to need ten: $1M ARR at 80% margins gives $800K profit with no outside funding.
items.angle: The bottleneck has moved from labor to trust, so distribution and in-person relationships become the scarce asset. That's deflationary for billable-hour professions.
items.tweetA: A 60–90x productivity gain in immigration law, and the company's plan is 350 in-person events. When AI makes the work free, trust is what you're selling.
items.tweetB: Two-person software companies with $800K profit don't raise VC, don't hire, and don't show up in payroll data. That's a labor-market blind spot.

items.title: Baidu's Robin Li warns of an AI bubble and pitches a 'Token Exchange' to ease compute shortages
items.idea: Robin Li said most companies have yet to generate meaningful revenue or profit from AI investment, and that spending must turn into profit to avoid a bubble. He expects the application layer to capture the most value. Baidu's Token Exchange is meant to ease computing shortages, in effect a market for inference capacity.
items.angle: A Chinese hyperscaler CEO talking bubble while building a compute exchange is a sign of tokens becoming a commodity. Compute-as-commodity markets are where pricing power goes.
items.tweetA: China's answer to the GPU shortage isn't more GPUs, it's a market for tokens. Once compute trades like a commodity, its price can fall like one. $BIDU
items.tweetB: The Baidu CEO calling a bubble from inside the compute-constrained market is notable. China is short GPUs and still sees overbuild risk.

items.title: New funds: Plural €1B, Sofinnova €725M, and two Africa-focused funds closing in a risk-off tape
items.idea: Plural raised €1B for its third early-stage fund and an opportunities vehicle (European tech). Sofinnova closed €725M for late-stage life sciences. Africa-focused vehicles also closed: Saviu II at €40M (Francophone Africa) and First Circle's $26M Africa fintech fund. Also: Bharat Semi raised a $24M seed for single-chip AI image sensors (design wins with General Atomics, Kaynes) and promises ≥70% system cost cuts.
items.angle: European and frontier-market VC is raising while US AI equities sell off, a sign that capital is diversifying away from US AI concentration.
items.tweetA: Plural closing €1B while the Nasdaq is down 15% matches the MUFG point: Europe's low AI exposure is starting to look like a feature to allocators.
items.tweetB: An Indian startup with a General Atomics design win for AI image sensors. India's semiconductor push is getting defense customers before consumer ones.

items.title: Ironsides: AI capex peaked in rate-of-change terms in 1Q26, and this cycle lands between the internet bust and shale
items.idea: Ironsides frames the correction as the Fed tightening into slowing earnings growth. The rate of change in AI infrastructure capex peaked with 1Q26 reports, and accommodative policy plus generous tax incentives encouraged malinvestment. Because the biggest spenders are financially strong, this cycle should sit between the internet and shale booms: a long tail rather than a 2000-style sudden stop. They lean toward a 2027 equity recovery, but not before 2Q27, and only after a Fed pivot and a bottom in negative earnings momentum.
items.angle: The 'shale, not dot-com' framing argues for owning the balance-sheet-strong spenders and avoiding the levered suppliers.
items.tweetA: Dot-com was funded by equity, shale by junk bonds, and AI by free cash flow from the most profitable companies ever. That's why the bust will be slow. Slow busts hurt the suppliers most.
items.tweetB: Peak capex growth was 1Q26, and markets topped in October. The lag between the second derivative and the price was about 6 months. Apply it to the recovery: earnings momentum bottoms, then ~2 quarters later, stocks.

items.title: Housing is breaking while consumption holds; S&P hit its correction objective, but capitulation hasn't happened
items.idea: Purchase applications, pending sales, builder sentiment and permits all point to weaker housing demand and supply. Retail sales revisions show consumption still resilient, though an equity wealth shock could hurt the holidays. The S&P correction target has been reached, but volatility, correlation and risk measures don't show capitulation. Likely path: a Thanksgiving-week bounce, then a retest or marginal new low around the Dec 9 FOMC. Ironsides is holding cash but tempted to catch falling knives if Monday follows through.
items.angle: A specific timing roadmap: tactical long into Thanksgiving, de-risk before Dec 9. Homebuilders are the place where the macro damage is already showing.
items.tweetA: Housing data is collapsing on both demand and supply and the Fed is still hiking on retail sales. That's a central bank looking backward at the consumer and ignoring the sector that drives the cycle. $ITB
items.tweetB: Bounce through Thanksgiving, retest into the Dec 9 FOMC. Krinsky, Ironsides and MacroEdge all landed on roughly the same path independently. When everyone agrees on the retest, it usually comes early or not at all.

items.title: The surge in Fed speeches signals little support for Warsh's rebalancing
items.idea: Ironsides reads the flood of Fed speeches as evidence of limited internal backing for Warsh's plan: looser rate and regulatory policy alongside a tighter balance sheet. That mix looks unlikely until markets force it. They also call the FOMC's lack of capital-markets experience a persistent blind spot and argue forward guidance was a tool for the zero lower bound and is now obsolete.
items.angle: A divided FOMC adds variance to the December decision and to 2027 guidance. Expect messy communication and higher rates vol.
items.tweetA: When a new chair's colleagues all start giving speeches, they aren't amplifying him, they're hedging against him. Warsh doesn't have the committee yet.
items.tweetB: Warsh wants lower rates plus a smaller balance sheet. The committee is giving him higher rates plus the same balance sheet. That's the worst combination for long-duration assets. $MOVE

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom (BTIG Krinsky)
items.title: Krinsky: six straight down days, sentiment at prior-low levels, but breadth damage isn't done and Apple won't crack
items.idea: The S&P 500 has fallen six sessions in a row, its longest losing streak since April 2024, and is nearing a key technical area. Sentiment and volatility gauges are at levels seen near past lows. Krinsky warns the breadth divergence shows the correction hasn't caused the broad technical damage that usually marks a durable bottom. Apple's resilience suggests the final washout may still be ahead.
items.angle: A tactical long for a bounce is reasonable, but durable bottoms need generals like $AAPL to capitulate. Watch Apple as the last shoe.
items.tweetA: The bottom isn't in while $AAPL is holding up. Durable lows need the last safe-haven megacap to get sold. Apple is the market's final hiding place, and nobody's been forced out yet.
items.tweetB: Six-day losing streaks with extreme fear usually mark tactical lows. But fear without breadth damage means everyone hedged and nobody sold. That leads to a bounce, not a bottom.

items.title: Meisler's Chart Fest: DSI at 9 on SPX, Nasdaq, gold and palladium; head-and-shoulders targets hit; bank index now down on the year
items.idea: Head-and-shoulders patterns worked and some hit targets, and the spring gaps are being filled. Daily Sentiment Index is at 9 (extreme bearish) on SPX, Nasdaq, GLD and PALL. QQQ, IWM and SOX are sitting at the top of their gaps. The bank index filled its gap but formed an H&S top and is down on the year. XBI's H&S is in play, OIH has broken, ITB looks unlike everything else, and INDA is the chart 'no one is talking about'. The McClellan Summation Index is heading down and the 10dma put/call is finally getting up there.
items.angle: DSI 9 across equities and metals at the same time is a contrarian bounce signal, but banks breaking an H&S is the credit-stress tell to respect.
items.tweetA: DSI at 9 on the S&P, Nasdaq, gold and palladium at once. When everything is equally hated, the bounce is usually violent and short. The bank index rolling over is the part that isn't sentiment.
items.tweetB: Meisler's quiet line: 'INDA. No one is talking about this.' While everyone watches the Nasdaq gap fill, India is the chart nobody is positioned for. $INDA

items.title: Google Cloud +103% y/y to $30.7B in Q3 2026 at a 36% margin, and Search is now under half of Alphabet's revenue
items.idea: Alphabet passed a half-trillion-dollar run rate: Q3 2026 revenue was $127.6B, of which Search was $63.4B (<50%). Cloud grew 103% y/y to $30.7B with $11.1B operating profit (36.2% margin), against $58.7B for all of 2025. Gemini 4 Argon/Carbon process ~32bn tokens per minute via API. Capex was $51.4B in the quarter and $131B+ YTD.
items.angle: Cloud alone is now a ~$120B run rate growing 100%. The 'Search disruption' bear case misses where the earnings are coming from.
items.tweetA: Google Cloud's Q3 alone was more than half of its entire 2025. Search is now less than half of Alphabet. The 'AI kills Google' trade got the direction right and the company wrong. $GOOGL
items.tweetB: $51B capex in a quarter, funded by $160B of ad cash flow. Ironsides' 'long tail, not sudden stop' thesis in one company: the strongest spender can't be forced to stop.

items.title: TPU supply-chain shift: moving generations to MediaTek cuts ASIC gross margin from ~65% (Broadcom) to ~35%, with full COT by 2030
items.idea: Alphabet is moving TPU generations toward MediaTek to protect its own margins, reducing ASIC partner gross margins from ~65% with Broadcom to ~35%, and is targeting full Customer-Owned Tooling by 2030. TPU v7 Ironwood links up to 9,216 chips in one optical domain, and TPU system sales are now reported as direct product revenue inside Cloud.
items.angle: A direct margin threat to $AVGO's custom-silicon franchise, and a template other hyperscalers can copy. It's a tailwind for MediaTek and for optical interconnect.
items.tweetA: The biggest risk to $AVGO isn't fewer AI ASICs, it's customers who learn to build them. 65% → 35% gross margin is Google telling every hyperscaler what the Broadcom tax costs.
items.tweetB: 9,216 TPUs in one optical domain. Google is selling TPU systems as products now. Nvidia's real competitor doesn't sell GPUs, it sells clusters.

items.title: Alphabet's other engines: YouTube passes 150M paid subs, Waymo takes a $16B round, and there are 500+ subsidiaries in 60 countries
items.idea: YouTube ads bring in $11.2B a quarter, and subscriptions, devices and platforms did $48.0B in 2025 and $14.3B in Q3 2026. YouTube Music/Premium passed 150M paying subscribers. Alphabet anchored a $16B Waymo round in early 2026 to fund Zeekr and Ioniq 5 fleets against Uber and Tesla. The structure: 3 SEC-registered holding subs (Google LLC, XXVI Holdings, Alphabet Capital US) branching into 500+ operating entities. Insights come from 15 insider interviews (Search, Gemini, YouTube, DeepMind, AlphaChip, Waymo, DV360).
items.angle: Subscription and Waymo optionality is under-modeled sum-of-the-parts value in a correction.
items.tweetA: YouTube has 150M paying subscribers and is the dominant TV streamer. It would be one of the largest media companies on earth as a standalone. Inside Alphabet it's a footnote to Cloud.
items.tweetB: Waymo's $16B round comes in the same year Nvidia's founder is in front of Congress. The autonomy race is being financed by whoever has ad cash flow. $UBER $TSLA

items.title: The Anthropic IPO stabilization is reportedly exhausted: the greenshoe is used up and the stock has no net
items.idea: Paulo Macro, a 25-year ECM veteran, initially doubted a Reuters report, then confirmed that Anthropic's IPO stabilization (the greenshoe) has been exhausted. The syndicate can no longer support the stock in the aftermarket. He explains the structure: base deal X, a 15% greenshoe for stabilization, and sometimes a 'hot issue' upsizing of ~20% (up to 50%). He calls the IPO the 'AOL-Time Warner bell' for the AI cycle.
items.angle: With the greenshoe used up, the syndicate bid is gone. Price discovery is now pure supply and demand ahead of lockups, so expect volatility in Anthropic and in AI comps.
items.tweetA: The greenshoe is the underwriters' insurance policy, and it's already spent on the biggest IPO ever. From here Anthropic trades with no syndicate bid, into a market down 15%.
items.tweetB: An exhausted greenshoe means the syndicate bought back its overallotment to hold the price, so the deal needed support. Busted mega-IPOs mark cycle tops. Ask Facebook in 2012, or AOL in 2000.

items.title: The Wallenberg playbook: Investor AB has matched US tech since 2008, after 110 years of patient capital
items.idea: Blind Squirrel looked at Sweden's Investor AB, the listed vehicle of the Wallenberg dynasty, founded in 1916 with Stockholms Enskilda Bank's industrial assets and listed in 1917. Holding minority stakes in a few global industrials, it has delivered returns comparable to US tech since 2008. The frame is 'clogs to clogs in three generations' (shirtsleeves in the US, sandals in Japan): most family wealth dissipates, so the families that compound over centuries are worth studying.
items.angle: Swedish family holdcos are a diversifier from US tech with similar long-run returns, and they often trade at a NAV discount.
items.tweetA: Since 2008, a 110-year-old Swedish family holding company has kept pace with US tech without owning any. In an AI unwind, the patient money may end up winning. $INVE-B
items.tweetB: Most family fortunes go 'clogs to clogs' in three generations. The Wallenbergs are on generation five-plus. Governance is an asset class, and markets rarely price it.
